processing: Sun-dried large-leaf maocha steamed and pressed into cakes, as was usual for the private Yiwu tea houses of its era. The surviving tea has had around a century of natural ageing.
harvest_season: Not documented for individual lots. No modern harvest exists for the original house, which belongs to the pre-1957 era.
appearance_dry: As with other antique pu-erh, a very dark, aged cake with brown-black leaf, and a paper label that matters as much as the tea to buyers.
appearance_liquor: Typical of very old sheng, a deep chestnut to red-brown and clear when well stored.
appearance_wet: As with other long-aged sheng, soft dark brown leaf, with little of the original green left.
taste_profile: Reliable tasting notes are scarce because so few people have drunk it. Expect what is typical of very old dry-stored sheng: woody, earthy and soft, without the bitterness of a young cake.

brewing.notes: General advice for very old sheng: one quick rinse, water near the boil, and a clay or thick porcelain pot to hold the heat.

vintage_note: This is not a tea you buy by harvest: it trades as single antique cakes and whole seven-cake bundles at specialist auctions, described by label and by era. Red-label pieces are marketed as about a century old. Any cheap or newly pressed tea using the name is at best a modern tribute and has no link to those antiques by default.
description:
Songpin Hao is a name from pu-erh's antique age, one of the private family tea houses whose pre-1957 cakes are now called antique or hao-level tea. It is not a style you can shop for so much as a historical label, spoken of in the same breath as Tongqing Hao and Tongchang Hao.

The houses of this period worked around Yiwu, and their tea is thought to have come from the six famous mountains nearby. Output was small and quality varied from one house and one production to the next. Details of how Songpin itself made its tea are not well recorded, so the safest assumption is the general method of the time: sun-dried leaf, steamed and pressed into cakes.

Few drinkers will ever taste one, and most descriptions come from people with something to sell. What is typical of very old sheng is softness, wood and earth, and a long quiet finish. If you ever get a sample, treat it gently: a small amount, a quick rinse and short steeps.

The market is the most documented part of the story. Red-label Songpin has sold at Hong Kong auction for millions of Hong Kong dollars, with a single cake hammered at HK$3.5 million in 2024 and a whole bundle of seven later passing HK$20 million. Prices like that attract fakes, so provenance matters more than any label.

To get a sense of this flavour family without an auction paddle, try a well-stored Yiwu sheng of twenty years or more.
history:
Songpin Hao is listed among the antique teas, the private house productions from before 1957. Those businesses clustered around Yiwu from the start of the 20th century and sent tea on to Tibet, Beijing, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia.

Little is reliably documented about the house's founders. Its modern fame rests largely on surviving cakes, which auction houses date to about a century ago, the best known being the red label.
